speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS WITH COSTA RICA, HONDURAS, NICARAGUA, PANAMA AND ECUADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform hon. members that the Canadian government and the governments of the republics of Costa Rica, Honduras, Nicaragua and Panama have agreed to establish diplomatic relations. The Canadian ambassador to these four republics will be appointed shortly. He will normally reside in San Jose, Costa Rica, but will spend some time each year in the capitals of the three other republics to which he will be concurrently accredited: Managua, Nicaragua, Tegucigalpa, Honduras and Panama City, Panama. The four governments have indicated their intention to be represented in Ottawa by giving double accreditation to their ambassadors to neighbouring countries until such time as resident ambassadors can be appointed to Canada.
I wish also to announce that the Canadian government and the government of the republic of Ecuador have agreed to exchange ambassadors. The Canadian ambassador to Columbia, Mr. Jean Morin, will be accredited as Canadian ambassador to Ecuador. Mr. Morin will continue to serve as Canadian ambassador to Columbia and will normally reside in Bogota but will spend some time each year in Quito. During the ambassador's absence from Quito, the Canadian embassy in Ecuador will be under a resident charge d'affaires ad interim. The Canadian government is looking forward to receiving the first Ecuadorean ambassador to Canada in the near future.
Representation at this high level reflects the intention of the Canadian government and of the governments concerned to strengthen and improve diplomatic, cultural and commercial relations. It is a further recognition of the importance of the growing ties between Canada and Latin America.
Finally, hon. members will be pleased to learn that the Canadian government has now formally accepted an invitation from the council of the Organization of American
States to send an observer to the eleventh inter-American conference, which will be held at Quito later this year.

The article in question refers to the program of building regional centres for emergency purposes in wartime. That program was announced by me on May 31, 1960 and in the announcement I set forth in part the situation in these words, which will be found at page 4359 of Hansard of that date:
The plan is to provide in each province a centre from which a small core of federal, provincial and army personnel can direct emergency operations within the province, even in the presence of radioactive fall-out, the loss of normal means of communication and possibly the destruction of some provincial capitals.

Regional centres will be established speedily in each of the provinces.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, January 17, consideration of the motion of Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Benidickson.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already indicated my approval of the budget proposals which, coupled with the governments's legislative program, will do much for the national economy and to stimulate employment. I have a proposal to present to the house-perhaps you might call it an idea-which I believe would more closely be the next logical step in this development. In presenting this proposal I hope that hon. members will permit me to refer to my notes more closely than usual.
I wish to call this plan the Canadian products plan. It is a plan designed to improve the Canadian internal economy and to make better provision for those Canadians on welfare assistance. It is put forward as a beginning only, and can be enlarged and developed to encompass additional segments of the economy as circumstances require.
The plan is based on several assumptions. First, Canada is rich in food, clothing and products for shelter and comfort, all the basic necessities of life. There is no economic reason why any needy person should be deprived of these basics. However, it is much too simple to literally reach into our wheat bins for bread, into our orchards for fruit and into our mills for lumber and textiles. On the other hand the mere handing out of increasing sums of money to be spent in an economy overbalanced with imported goods, makes the situation worse instead of better. We must find a way to get our Canadian

The Budget-Mr. Aiken products into the hands of the welfare recipients for the benefit of the Canadian economy which provides both products and money.
The second assumption is that the needs of those receiving welfare payments are constantly on the increase in an expanding economy. The government is now facing demands from all sides for increased welfare and pension benefits in order to maintain recipients on the standards reached even three years ago. These demands will have to be met, and in the course of the development of human betterment policies, new categories may be created in the future.
The third assumption is that in the past, two methods have been attempted in order to sell Canadian products to the Canadian public. The first has been the control of imports by arbitrary methods such as tariffs. Experience has shown the futility of relying solely upon such external pressures. We are a trading nation, and we must not jeopardize our export markets. We are also legally bound by the general agreement on tariffs and trade, and the cumbersome methods of international amendment make external changes difficult.
The second method has been that of trying to stop Canadians from buying imports with "buy Canadian" campaigns and by appealing to the patriotism of the public to buy Canadian, even if the product costs a few cents more. Sad as it may seem, these appeals largely fail. A housewife working on a limited budget is more interested in saving a few cents here and there than in inquiring about the source of the product.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I should like to ask for a little better attention for him. There seems to be more conversation than usual going on in the house. I hope hon. members will give the hon. member who has the floor a courteous hearing.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am presenting what I consider to be a very important and even spectacular proposal. It may not be as interesting to listen to as some of the debates we have, but I feel it is a proposal that deserves very serious consideration.
The situation of the housewife in trying to save money here and there applies even more to welfare recipients. We must, therefore, devise a plan to be applied internally in Canada, without imposing direct trade barriers, to provide recipients with an incentive to buy Canadian products. This will provide Canadian markets for the industries and producers who are paying the taxes, without depriving them of their export markets. Quite aside, Mr. Speaker, from the

question of welfare payments, it is surely a basic principle that when public funds raised by Canadian taxes are being used in public works the content of such works must be Canadian in order to provide full employment and continuing tax revenues.
My plan is divided into two separate parts. The first I call the Canadian products incentive plan. Simply stated, this plan would provide for payment by the federal government to pensioners of a bonus, which I have set arbitrarily for the moment at 10 per cent, on all purchases of certified Canadian products made with pension or welfare funds. The plan would extend to non-contributory pensions provided or subsidized in whole or in part by the government of Canada, including such welfare payments as old age security, family allowances, veterans pensions, war veterans allowances, old age assistance, blind and disabled persons pensions. This plan, if it were thought fit, could also be extended to contributory allowances such as military, R.C.M.P. and civil service pensions and unemployment insurance, or to any other segment of the economy as circumstances might require.
This plan would envisage first the setting up of a Canadian products certification board; second, setting up a paying authority and, third, the application of the plan to such Canadian products as are required for food, clothing, shelter and household furnishings but not including items generally regarded as luxuries.
The second part of this plan would be called the Canadian products requirement plan. This would require that all materials provided and labour performed in buildings and works for which the federal government provides funds or lends funds in whole or in part shall be Canadian labour and Canadian products as defined by the Canadian products certification board. This plan would extend to residential or commercial buildings constructed under the National Housing Act, with industrial development bank loans or with any other public funds of Canada, and would apply to all contracts for public works awarded by the government of Canada, defence contracts for armaments not available in Canada excepted. Where Canadian products are not available or for aesthetic reasons imported materials are considered advisable or necessary, non-Canadian products up to 15 per cent of the total contract amount could be used, but a penalty of 10 per cent of the cost of such non-Canadian goods would be imposed, payable to the paying authority under the Canadian products plan. This plan could be extended to any other classification

of public spending now or hereafter established, such as the small business loans recently provided by the house.
In connection with administration, simplicity of administration is a primary object of the plan. There would be three separate phases of administration, the first being classification of products. For this purpose a new agency known as the Canadian products certification board would have to be established. Every manufacturer or producer of a Canadian product could apply to the board for a certificate bearing an identifying number upon proof that any described product is a Canadian product. Where practical, a distinctive marker bearing the certificate number could be applied to the product or printed on the label. Otherwise the product would be identified by a certain certificate number.
The board could classify products as Canadian in the following manners or in such other manner as they may adopt:
1.	Products wholly produced, processed, fabricated, packaged and distributed in Canada.
2.	Products not native to or normally produced in Canada, which are in common use and accepted as necessaries, and which are imported into Canada in raw form and wholly fabricated, processed, packaged and distributed in Canada so that at least 50 per cent of wholesale cost is developed in Canada, and for which there is not a similar product or substitute available in Canada.
3.	Products fabricated, processed, packaged and distributed in Canada, partly of imported raw products and partly of Canadian raw products, provided that the Canadian raw content be not less than equal value with the imported raw product.
The second phase would require certification of purchase. One might ask how, if these products are so classified, purchasing would be controlled and on what basis. My plan would be that every retail dealer in Canada could apply for and receive authority to act as a certifying agent under the act, with the appropriate responsibilities. Upon request such retail dealer would provide a purchaser with a separate invoice or sales slip for certified Canadian products, giving the identifying number of each item and certifying that all goods shown on such invoice were Canadian products certified under the act. Wholesalers dealing directly with contractors could obtain similar entitlement.
As to payment, having established that the recipient had purchased a Canadian product, attached to each cheque issued under the Old Age Security Act or other qualifying statute would be a duplicate or additional voucher, in the form of a carbon copy if required, certifying that such payment qualifies for bonus
The Budget-Mr. Aiken under the Canadian products incentive plan and giving the date, amount, pension number and name of payee. This voucher, when accompanied by properly certified invoices of purchase, would support payment by the paying authority. In the event of doubt, however, the name and pension number would permit speedy cross reference.
The bonus cheque issued as the result of this payment would be redeemable in certified Canadian products at an authorized dealer's premises, and would bear a printed endorsement so certifying for signature by such dealer. The paying authority could be either a special branch in existing paying offices or a special authority set up under the plan, and possibly quarterly applications would be more convenient to handle rather than monthly.
Under the Canadian products requirement plan, the second of those I have mentioned, final payment of any loan or contract amount would require certification by the architect, government inspector or other supervising agent that the provisions of the plan had been complied with. This plan, Mr. Speaker, has a number of direct objectives. They are:
1.	To move toward self-sufficiency in Canada, commencing with the welfare field where the taxpayers, the Canadian public are providing the funds.
2.	To grant welfare increases on a useful basis.
3.	To stimulate Canadian production in a natural manner.
4.	To stimulate employment by the creation of industries to supply the market.
5.	To restore trade balances by internal application and without special tariffs.
6.	To mark clearly Canadian products and make the public conscious of them.
7.	To establish the habit of purchasing Canadian products, with a bonus incentive. Such habit may naturally extend to normal purchases. I should add, Mr. Speaker, that it would only be welfare or other federal government funds to which this plan would apply initially.
8.	To establish a system which could be extended into other categories as circumstances indicate.
9.	With regard to the Canadian products requirement plan, to circulate public funds strictly within the national economy so that employment and taxes would be created for the benefit of the national economy.
10.	To offer a bonus incentive for the purchase of Canadian goods, but providing no limitation on the freedom of spending.
11.	The plan would not underwrite excessive prices of uneconomical Canadian production. If the price were too high, this 10 per cent

The Budget-Mr. Aiken incentive bonus would be applied to other Canadian products or to competitive or noncompetitive products.
Now, with these objectives in mind and with this background plan, we have to consider whether there would be any real impact on the Canadian economy. My effort is to set up a system whereby within Canada the spending would be upon Canadian goods by those people who receive the benefit of public assistance. I feel this is the only fair way in which such public spending can be justified. The value of the foregoing plan would depend entirely upon its impact on the economy. I have used the dominion bureau of statistics booklet, national accounts, income and expenditure 1959, which is the latest booklet, also the Bank of Canada statistical summary, financial supplement, 1959, and the 1959-60 spending found in the estimates.
Now, referring to the estimates and to these booklets, we find the following figures. Personal expenditures on consumer goods in Canada in 1959 amounted to $14,058 million; personal expenditures on consumer services, to $8,203 million, making a total expenditure on consumer goods and services of $22,261 million. Comparing that with the total of consumer goods imported into Canada, as found in the bank summary, page 153, we find that amounted to $1,799 million. Then I should like to relate this to the welfare payments and other payments that potentially would come under the incentive plan. We find that the federal government's transfer and welfare payments, not including interest, as shown on the dominion bureau of statistics table 44, amount to $1,801 million. We find that all governments, federal, provincial and municipal, have transfer and welfare payments, not including interest, amounting to $2,785 million.
Taking first the Canadian products incentive plan, we find that imports of consumer goods amounted to about 12.8 per cent of the total expenditure on consumer goods in Canada. Therefore if we assume that the federal government contributes directly or indirectly to all government welfare spending, which amounts to $2,785 million, we can assume that 12.8 per cent thereof or $356.4 million of goods would be purchased in Canada under this plan which would otherwise be imported. This is relating the plan solely to imported goods and solely to the spending of the Canadian public who are welfare recipients.
Taking next the Canadian products requirement plan, that is the plan under which you would require absolute use of Canadian products in all government supported spending, we turn to the figures on gross national expenditure as found in the dominion bureau of statistics booklet at page 20. We find that

imports of goods and services valued at $8,065 million represent about 18.9 per cent of the gross national expenditure of $42,655 million. We find also that government spending represents 15.1 per cent of the imports of goods and services of $8,065 million, which is $1,217 million that would be redirected into the local market.
These two figures, while no doubt subject to error adjustments because of factors which are not obvious to me, total $1,574 million, which is more than sufficient to balance the 1959 international current account deficit which amounts to $1,429 million. It may be said that much of the incentive plan funds would be spent on Canadian goods which would have been purchased anyway. This is true, and in fact the above figures are based on the premise that Canadian goods are normally purchased in 87.2 per cent of the cases anyway. It is the other 12.8 per cent which would make the difference. These are estimates of the amounts of goods and services imported into Canada which are purchased with welfare funds. The same applies to the requirements plan in somewhat a different ratio.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have given a great deal of thought to this matter over the last couple of years. As I stated at the outset, this is not the sort of speech that one finds perhaps as interesting as others which have been made in this debate. However, I have had a feeling for some time that we were moving in the wrong direction in connection with such things as welfare spending and Canadian products. I feel that this plan could be extended. The welfare field is only a beginning, and it is a logical beginning because we have the goods, we have the national assets and in addition the money is coming from the Canadian taxpayer and the Canadian manufacturer. There is no reason why this money should not be used for the purchase of Canadian products.
However, I recognize the fact that you cannot force people to do things in a free economy. You cannot force them to go out and buy Canadian products. For this reason I feel it is better for the increase in welfare payments to be by way of a bonus incentive to buy Canadian products. In this way the funds will be used for the benefit of the Canadian economy.
By way of summary may I say that the total cost of this plan to the federal government would be a 10 per cent increase in welfare payments. As I stated, this is an arbitrary figure. It might very well be more. However, it is the amount which I feel will be required immediately. All of this increase of 10 per cent will be funnelled back into the Canadian economy. It must be funnelled:

back because it is redeemable only for Canadian products. In addition to the 10 per cent which will be funnelled back, 100 per cent of the basic payment will also be funnelled back into the Canadian economy because it is with these funds that purchases of Canadian products will be made. Those people who prefer to use imported products will be free to do so. They merely will not qualify for the bonus. I feel that the administrative costs would not be heavy, requiring only the establishment of the certification board. I would not anticipate any payments to retail merchants because their appointment and duties would be a matter of routine. Their appointment as agents would be of benefit to themselves as well as to those people who are purchasing these products.
The benefit of the plan, however, could be of the financial order which I have already set out. If correct, this sum would be sufficient to offset our international deficit on trade balances. I think this plan can offer an incentive for new businesses and an expansion of existing businesses which would coincide with the announced plans of the government and which are, in fact, in the legislative program for this session.
I am submitting this plan for consideration. If my figures are in error, then the extent of the initial impact may be varied or may be less than I have stated. However, the application of the idea would still be just as valid.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposiiion):
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister reminded us this morning that this debate roams or can roam over all aspects of the state of the nation. When I use the expression "state of the nation" I do not mean that caricature of the state of the nation which was obtained from the Prime Minister the other evening on television, when he confirmed once again the thesis that seems to be held by himself and so many of his colleagues and supporters, namely that the history of Canada began three years or so ago.
It is quite true that some bad history began at that time. It is not true-and it is a caricature of history to try to make it true-that the expansion and the development of this country ended with Right Hon. R. B. Bennett and began again in June, 1957 after 22 years of sterility and stagnation. The answer to that thesis, Mr. Speaker, was given very well the other day in a speech from which I will quote just one sentence. That sentence is this:
In past years-
The Budget-Mr. Pearson
I may say that this speech was made on January 9.
-when our economic capacities were stretched to the limit in the process of unprecedented economic expansion-*
Unprecedented expansion in past years.
-we supplemented our own resources both financial and physical with goods and capital from abroad but today our resources are not stretched.
That statement, which is a true one was made on January 9, 1961, in Toronto by the Minister of Finance, whose past statements seem to be arising to haunt him these days.
When we discuss this special budget, this baby budget or whatever you wish to call it, the first question we ask ourselves, of course, is why there is a special budget at this time at all in view of the fact that the government denies that there is any special emergency which would require this kind of special treatment. Of course a special budget in December gave the minister an opportunity, if he had desired to take advantage of it, to recant his wrong predictions of earlier months. I suppose it would have been a little bit less embarrassing for him to do that in December than to do it in March or in April when the regular budget would be introduced, and when he might well have even more to recant than he had last December.
He took a more realistic view of the economy in his speech last December-I am referring to the Minister of Finance-than he did earlier in the year, but his confession of mistaken predictions was certainly only partial. He was less naively optimistic than in his budget speech in March, but he still flatly refused to recognize or to admit the seriousness of the situation which this country now faces. That makes his position now only a little bit less realistic than his optimistic predictions of a few months ago made it.
With ignorance of what was happening then and with a refusal to face the facts now, the proposals which have been put forward by the government are naturally inadequate to deal with this situation of employment emergency which they deny. Of course the Prime Minister and his supporters may get some comfort out of the statement by the Prime Minister the other night that the situation was worse in 1936 and 1937. It certainly was worse in 1936 and 1937.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Up until 1940.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At that time the Liberal government inherited a situation with 17 per cent or 18 per cent of the labour force unemployed, and it took a few years to get that figure down.

The Budget-Mr. Pearson

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It took a war.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If he would not be misleading in these comparisons, let the Prime Minister take comparable figures in the last 10 or 12 years and see whether the Canadian people will get any comfort out of those figures in comparison with the present emergency.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the Leader of the Opposition permit a question?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If his party inherited that situation in 1935, what does he think the Conservative party inherited in 1930?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In 1930 the Conservative party inherited the beginning of a great depression; and when the Conservative party left office in 1935, after promising to cure that depression, it was worse than ever.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is definitely not a fact.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The question arises as to where the Minister of Finance gets the information on which he bases his economic forecasts. The main source of this information used to be the report known as the Canadian economic outlook, that report which we know as a confidential document which we were accused of hiding in 1957 and which, after removal of the word "confidential", was in that year made public in carefully selected passages out of context.
What has happened to that report now? It has been abolished, destroyed and buried. The reason is quite obvious. The kind of economic analysis and economic information based on the researches of experts, the kind of prediction of trends which would appear in a report of that kind now would be extremely embarrassing to the government as a reminder of their own false predictions and inadequate actions. Therefore the report has been cancelled.
If the Minister of Finance took a somewhat more realistic view of the situation in December than he did in earlier months of the year, he is still not prepared to admit that there is a recession in this country. Indeed, the very idea of a recession was denied very vigorously by his parliamentary secretary in his contribution to this debate.
"There is no recession", say the minister and his parliamentary secretary, echoing other members of the government, including the Prime Minister, who told us last spring and summer that all was well, that we were going through a pause out of which we would soon emerge, and that in 1960 everything was going up and up and on and on in the

economy. He also told us that the gross national product would be up 6 per cent in 1960. That was the prediction, and that we would have a surplus, after successive deficits, of $12 million. We all remember the banging of desks when that announcement was made in the House of Commons, a banging and excitement which was only equalled a little later in New York by Mr. Khrushchev when he banged his desk at the United Nations.
Those members who took part in the debate last spring and summer will remember that we on this side refused to accept this easy optimism of the government spokesmen. We warned the minister at that time-and he must be aware of the warning-that his rosy predictions were not likely to be realized. In return for these warnings, which have turned out to be correct, we were accused of being prophets of gloom and doom.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Correct.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We were accused of being prophets of gloom and doom, and last March, April, May, June and July we were accused of selling Canada short.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Correct.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We were accused of being subversive; it was said that we must not mention these difficulties and dangers. Well, who was right last spring and summer, and who was wrong? Who was blind? Who were the false prophets?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You were.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who had their heads in the sand last spring and last summer, and who now worship the sand their heads are buried in? Let the facts speak. We said the gross national product would not likely be up 6 per cent. We warned the minister it would not; and what are the figures?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It went up just the same.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It went up just the same; it went up by 2.9 per cent in value in the first nine months of last year and 1.6 per cent in volume, which is a far cry from the 6 per cent prediction on the basis of which the minister made his calculations for a surplus, which we told him at that time was unrealistic.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not a far cry
at all. Have some sense of proportion here.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There was an increase of 1.6 per cent in the volume of the gross national product, which itself is the explanation for the unemployment we are now suffering in this country. And the Prime Minister now tries to take our minds off this question of

unemployment by pointing out that we have the highest employment at the present time in the history of this country.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is true.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not true. It could not be less true. The dominion bureau of statistics figures for January 18, the day before the Prime Minister spoke on this matter, show that employment, not unemployment, decreased by 127,000 between November and December. Is it true, then, that we have the highest employment in our history, as the Prime Minister said?
Instead we have unemployment which is the highest in this country since the 1930's, and no manipulation of facts and figures by government spokesmen can alter that hard and cruel fact. The figures published on December 10 show that 528,000 men and women in this country are out of work. And these are figures with which we all agree; the dispute over calculations I hope is over. On the basis of agreed figures we have 528,000 people out of work, as compared with 406,000 a year ago. The figures show that 8.2 per cent of our labour force was out of work in December, as compared with 6.5 per cent a year ago, or indeed as compared with 7.6 per cent in 1958, when conditions were so bad.
In 1960 the per capita national production in this country was 5 per cent lower in volume than in 1956. If present trends continue, by March we might well have in this country 14 per cent of the labour force jobless and an unemployment insurance fund diminishing rapidly.
When we predicted this trend, as we did, we were jeered at. But unhappily our predictions have been shown to be correct-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and the minister's predictions almost invariably, in almost every respect, wrong. The seriousness of this problem which hon. gentlemen on the other side do not seem to yet realize is confirmed by even more significant quarter to quarter comparisons with 1960 made on the basis of seasonally adjusted figures at annual rates.
What do they show? They show that the picture is very different from that painted by the minister or the Prime Minister in March, July or last December. I know that in putting these official figures on the record we will again be accused of gloom and doom. The government would like to silence this kind of talk in this house, but there is no possibility of dealing with this situation unless the facts are made clear, until the government become aware of the facts and aware of the seriousness reflected by these facts. Until
The Budget-Mr. Pearson they are aware of these things, how can they possibly deal with a situation which they refuse to admit exists?
The first quarter of 1960 was relatively good; it was encouraging and it marked, I suppose, the peak of the 1957-59 cycle. During the second quarter the gross national product declined by 1.5 per cent, which was the first decline since the last quarter of 1957 and the biggest drop in any quarterly period in the post-war years. This record reduction marked the beginning of the 196061 recession and was accompanied by lower exports, mainly to the United States. Then during the third quarter of 1960 the overall depressed conditions of the second quarter continued to prevail, with one very significant change; the value of our exports during the third quarter increased by more than $400 million.
Since our gross national product remained at about the same level during those two quarters, it means that the domestic sector of our economy continued to weaken during the third quarter. We were saved, at that time at least, from a further over-all decline by increased exports, especially to Europe. This is the exact opposite of what the minister stated in his budget speech, when he attempted to blame our depressed conditions on external forces and on the slowing down of economic activity in Europe.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not true; that is not even half true.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister can interrupt all he likes, but he cannot deny the logic of facts and figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, the hon. gentleman is purporting to attribute certain statements to me. He has not chosen to read what I said. He is choosing to take some things I said and turn them as though they were all I said, and so I say his statement just now is not even a half truth.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That has nothing to do with privilege. We can easily get the position from the minister's speech. I have plenty of time, and I shall be very glad to take it. The minister left the impression, I repeat, and his words can convey no other impression, that one reason, indeed the major reason, for our present depressed condition was external forces in Europe and the United States. Does the minister deny that he gave that impression in his budget speech?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I reviewed the whole situation and I pointed out those factors both external and domestic which accounted for the change in conditions in

The Budget-Mr. Pearson Canada. I gave the whole story. If the hon, gentleman is going to attempt to deal with my remarks, I suggest that in all fairness and fidelity to the truth he should deal with them in a balanced way and not in this selective way.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am being perfectly fair to the Minister of Finance, and his own words will prove my fairness. He attributed our present depressed situation in large part to the European situation, and before I conclude I shall be able to put on the record exactly what he did say in that regard. In any event I should not have attributed to the minister words which mention our depressed situation, because the hon. gentleman does not admit we are in a recession. He says there is no recession in this country and in this, as I mentioned, he was echoed by his parliamentary secretary. But his view in this regard is denied by the Prime Minister, who the other night talked about "a recession which was foreseeable back in 1957"-a recession which, according to the Minister of Finance, does not exist.
Is there any outside, objective evidence on this point? Perhaps the minister does not feel we are objective witnesses to the existence or otherwise of a recession.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I certainly do not.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, let me put on record the views of some of the minister's friends, or at any rate the views of those who, if they are not his friends, have no reason to be unfriendly toward him. There is the Letter Review of Fort Erie, a respected publication, and it had this to say on December 26, 1960:
I960 has been a year of doubt, uncertainty, grave difficulties so far as Canadian economy is concerned. Unemployment has begun to haunt the country as at no time since the thirties.
Was the man who wrote that selling Canada short? Then there is the Toronto publication Saturday Night, which had this to say on January 7, 1961:
By any meaningful measurement, the Canadian economy is in recession.
Is the man who wrote that selling Canada short?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He was mistaken.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister has acquired the habit over the years of assuming that if he keeps on saying things often enough they become true, in his own mind at least. However, the facts are against him. Here is an American magazine, Fortune, an authoritative enough magazine in business and financial affairs, as the minister will at once admit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You have run out of
Canadian ones already?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are plenty of others, but I shall produce evidence from all over the world as well. Fortune had this to say:
In Canada nobody minces words about it-
I admit the author is wrong when he says nobody minces words about it.
The economy has run out of steam.
Canada is in a short term cyclical recession.
Then there is the evidence of the Economist and the Financial Times in London, and the Manchester Guardian, which is dismissed by the Prime Minister and by the minister as being founded on biased and inaccurate reports based on opposition speeches. It is really quite a tribute to the intelligence of these particular publications to say that they have been misled in their comments by what we have said in opposition in this house. That is the situation, Mr. Speaker, and the minister's budget shows no appreciation of it or of the need for emergency measures to get expansion going again.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if you could protect us from some of these chattering primitives on my left?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are referring to your own members, you know.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I remind the house that there is a good deal of interruption of the Leader of the Opposition from all parts of the chamber. This is not in accordance with the rules, and hon. members might recall that standing order No. 12, paragraph 3, specifically says:
When a member is speaking, no member shall interrupt him, except to raise a point of order.
I hope hon. members will take note of that and give the Leader of the Opposition the rights to which he is entitled.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you for intervening, Mr. Speaker. I hope that will make it a great deal easier for those members of the house who are so disposed to hear what I am saying.
The minister and his parliamentary secretary who take this optimistic view of the situation now, though it is not quite so optimistic as it was, have stated in this house, especially the parliamentary secretary, that the general reaction to this particular budget was most favourable and that everybody praised it. I do not wish to misquote the parliamentary secretary, but he was certainly very emphatic in his claim that there had been general and widespread approval of this particular budget. I could quote editorial after editorial in support of the

opposite view, but I will mention only two. The Vancouver Sun of December 22 stated:
Mr. Fleming's budget does not meet the needs of the economic crisis.
Indeed it does not. I might also quote the Conservative Globe and Mail of December 22, 1960 which said this:
It was his own optimism that led the minister astray back in March.
To this disappointment (falsification of his hopes) the Finance Minister has responded with a supplementary budget which itself is widely described as disappointing.
This particular budget was, of course, heralded in advance. It got a great build-up as dramatic evidence of the government's realization of the situation even at the last minute. We were led to believe that something exciting was going to be brought down. There were press predictions based on the usual informed sources that at last something really worth while was to be done about unemployment. Our hopes were deceived, as the minister's predictions were falsified earlier. There is nothing in this particular budget which deals in any adequate way with the unemployment emergency. Indeed, it increases the over-all tax burden. It fails to recognize the recession. It fails to recognize that there is an unemployment emergency. It is without planning or direction in dealing with this recession, this emergency. How could it be otherwise when the government is not aware of it?
There is, of course, a deficit now. The $12 million surplus is gone with the snows and we now have a $287 million deficit. But that is in no sense a planned deficit such as might have been justified at this time to deal with the emergency. How could it be a planned deficit when there was to be a surplus only a few months ago? This deficit is not the result of any policy decision brought about for the kind of purpose in a recession for which a deficit could be useful. It is not a remedy for a recession; it is the result of a recession. It is a very good example, to use the phrase of the parliamentary secretary, of budgeting by accident.
We shall be reviewing the proposals in this budget in detail when we get to the resolution stage. As my hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate has indicated, there are some good things in this budget. There are some proposals which may be very useful from the long range point of view even though there is nothing which could deal effectively with the emergency at the present time.
Even those good proposals, as we will point out when we come to discuss them in detail, are for the most part too limited, too little and too late. The special encouragement to small business is an example of this. The
The Budget-Mr. Pearson encouragement of new business activity in depressed areas is another example of something which is good in itself, but which is too limited in its application to deal with the situation we face at the present time. The proposed use of double depreciation is another example of something which is good in itself but, as we will point out, should go farther. If, for instance, this device is used merely to overcome temporary difficulties by accelerating development which would in any event occur, that effect will be purely temporary and inadequate.
Another measure which is good in principle but unsatisfactory in application is the tax concession offered in this budget to students and to parents of students. This particular measure is regressive in this sense, that it offers the most assistance to those who are in the best position to help themselves.
Then there are the proposals to discourage the inflow of foreign capital. The method adopted by the government in this budget is apparently to make it less attractive for nonresidents to invest their funds in Canada.
The Minister of Finance was pretty emphatic in New York the other day in telling his audience down there that it is not the purpose of the government in this budget or in any aspect of its financial policy-I think I am paraphrasing what he said-to discourage foreign investments, to discourage United States investors in particular. What is the particular provision if it is not to cut down on non-residents' investments in this country? One result of this is that it will be more expensive, not less expensive, for Canadians, especially the provinces and the municipalities, to finance their own needs.
I admit, Mr. Speaker, that it is difficult at this stage, of course, to assess the effect of the measures, but surely it is clear that they will increase the financial difficulties of the provinces and the municipalities. If they do seriously discourage long term foreign investment in this country, they will delay our development and they will delay that expansion which is so necessary for the cure of our present economic ills as well as for our long term prospects.

A restrictive credit policy designed to offset the consequences of the excessive creation of debt could go beyond the salutary checking of a boom to become a deterrent to normal and desirable economic growth.
He went on:
A policy which was necessary and inevitable when inflationary pressures were active may have been maintained too long and may even have been unsuited to a situation characterized by unemployed productive capacity and, more seriously, unemployed people.
We on this side agree with that statement, Mr. Speaker. That is why the method advocated by us in this present situation, which I have just mentioned, in our view is much better adapted to our present economic conditions. It is a method also advocated by many other respectable and experienced banking and financial experts. It would not discourage long term foreign investment, but it would prevent the inflow of international-* and I mentioned this when I spoke on the budget a year ago-hot money coming to Canada for speculative purposes only because of the higher interest rates prevailing in this country. Moreover, this method that we prefer would help meet the borrowing requirements of the provinces and the municipalities in a way that would reduce rather than increase their financial burdens. In our view the method proposed by the government is restrictive. It is likely to prolong the recession and the present stagnation. Our method is expansionist, and it would promote prosperity and growth.
I think, Mr. Speaker, the time has come to question the validity of traditional thinking on monetary and fiscal matters; the kind of thinking that keeps money tight and interest rates too high at a time of recession and high unemployment; the kind of thinking which relates, if you like, living beyond our means as a danger to this situation where half a million people in this country have no means

Mr. Speaker, we-and this has some bearing, no doubt, on what the Minister of Finance is driving at-would propose four fiscal measures, among others, which could be easily adjusted so that they could be brought to an end when the circumstances made that desirable.
The first one would be a temporary reduction of the rates of personal income tax. That is not-as the minister and others have indicated "In their public utterances-an irre-spoujibte"prBposal. It is a sound economic proposal for the present emergency situation.
This method of dealing with a recession is not new. We used it with good effect in this parliament in 1954 and 1955. We on this side advocated it in 1957 and 1958, when it was ignored by the government, who preferred what they called a billion dollar public works program. It is being advocated today by economic and financial experts in this country, a great many of them, objective economic expert?. It is being advocated today in the United States by the economic adviser to the new democrat administration, Professor Samuelson. It is being put forward by the governor of TTew York in the budget he is going to introduce in a few weeks time, and he is no long haired, left wing reformer. It is an eminently sound and sensible proposal to make in circumstances such as we face today, and only in those cir-*^Bsistances.	r-
Our second proposal would be that unemployment benefits should be increased for those taking vocational courses. That would have both an economic and a socially bene. ficial effect.
v-Our third fiscal measure would be accelerated depreciation allowances to help all business firms that wish to expand and put in new equipment, without the limitations placed on this device in the minister's proposal. <*. ' -^Ttur fourth measure would be that federal contributions to municipalities undertaking urban renewal projects should be increased - and broadened.	*4
These are all emergency, anti-recessionary and employment measures and they are put forward only in that sense. Other Liberal proposals which we have recently put forward do involve new, long term financial commitments, as contrasted with the emergency measures which I have just mentioned. Perhaps the most important of those would be a medical health plan.

The Budget-Mr. Pearson
But these long term measures, these long term proposals, should be implemented during an expanding and not a receding economy. That is the only way it can be done. But they should be implemented when the present emergency ends, because they correspond to the needs of Canada in the sixth decade of this country, and because in an expanding economy we can carry the financial burden that they involve. After all nobody can carry it but the taxpayers of this country.
As I have already said outside this house, all the money for these things, these long term measures and indeed the short term measures, comes out of one pocket, the taxpayer's pocket; and if we are going to take it out of his pocket-and in these circumstances that is the right course to adopt-* then we should arrange our economy so that we put more money in his pocket from which we can draw. Only then would the burden be supportable.
Careful and sound planned requirements with priorities should be established. The present unemployment emergency comes first. That is the greatest evil, the greatest social, economic and human evil that we have to face. That is why we Liberals advocate, as we have for three years now, an all-out planned attack against unemployment in order to get Canadians back to work. Such a program will be an emergency one and should be an emergency one. It will not be needed when our economy starts to move forward again and full employment has been restored.
There is one other subject which I wish to touch, because the minister devoted a good deal of time to it in his speech, and indeed in that speech he related it to the present position in Canada. I am referring to our export trade. While we have talked in this house during this debate mostly about domestic trade problems, it is impossible to underrate the importance of the problems of our external trading relationships.
The expansion of our exports is essential, and restrictionist policies which might prevent such expansion are bad and dangerous. I mentioned one of them this morning, and there are some others in this budget. We must do everything possible to encourage exports. Before I say a few words about the general problem I will make one concrete proposal. It is this; to encourage domestic manufacturing industries to increase their exports, tax incentives should be offered, including a reduction in corporation income tax on the profits earned on increased export sales.
It is quite clear to every member of this house that export trade is more important 

than ever. It is also encouraging and a cause for satisfaction that it has held up so well during 1960. But there are circumstances at the present time-and the minister has mentioned some of them-which give us some cause to worry about the prospects of export trade in 1961.
The trend in regard to our increase in exports over the years is interesting. The physical volume of exports rose between 1950 and 1953 by about 20 per cent. From 1953 to 1956 it rose 13 per cent, and from 1956 to 1959, 5 per cent. This year, as the minister has pointed out, an expanding European market proved, I do not think it is an exaggeration to call it so, a life-saver. But the United States market continues to be the most essential factor in the development of our export trade, and there are certainly dangers here. One danger would be to prejudice increased access to that market by adopting trade policies with regard to some other markets which, though they might have certain immediate benefits, might injure the long range development of our access to the United States market.
It is impossible to talk about the export trade and our markets abroad without talking about the regional associations which are now developing all over the world and particularly in Europe. There are today international trade developments taking place in the building up of regional trade associations, common markets and free trade areas which must disturb and, possibly, dislocate the customary pattern of multilateral trade from which Canada in the past has benefited as much as any single country in the world.
These developments, especially those in Europe, could have important and far-reaching potential effects politically and economically. They could also, as has been pointed out, if they are carried out in the wrong way, weaken instead of strengthen the free democratic countries, especially if they result in increasing rather than decreasing the obstacles to trade between the free nations within these associations and the free nations outside. That is true, but it is no good Canada or any other country trying to protect itself against that kind of result by giving irritated lectures to the British or other European governments on the sanctity of special arrangements.
Canada should take a very different kind of leadership in this matter in the advocacy of closer integration on the widest possible basis. We should seize that kind of initiative, help break through these European developments in the interest of making them Atlantic developments before it is too late. Surely, this is a strategic moment at which to do

this, with a new and forward looking administration taking office in Washington.
Surely this is the time-and it may not persist over many months-when we should make such a break through in the direction of converting these European associations into an association on a broader basis than that of Europe alone. We had a wonderful opportunity to begin that process in this country three years ago when the British made their free trade offer. That is gone. Let us try to manufacture new opportunities now, because if these developments take the wrong course we shall suffer more than perhaps any other country. Let us try to build up an Atlantic trade area with nations cooperating closely together in an association which would be open to others who might wish to join.
What has this government done in pursuing such an objective? It has threatened our friends in Europe that if they take certain steps we may have to retaliate. The Montreal Star of November 18 quotes the Minister of Finance as saying-and this speech has .been referred to already in this debate-that a common agricultural policy for Europe if adopted by the United Kingdom in whole or in part would be totally unacceptable. The report goes on to quote the minister as saying that if that happened:
-the pressure for Canada to embark on closer trade associations with other countries, particularly the United States, would understandably be increased.
I take it that is a kind of threat of massive retaliation.

Mr. Fleming must be very careful, however, not to become a victim of his own forthrightness. Retaliation has its place in international dealings but it can never substitute for policy. One would wish Mr. Fleming were more forthright about the alternatives. He does recognize at least one alternative-"Closer trade association with other countries, particularily the United States"-but there is no indication this would be any more satisfactory than retaliation.
A correspondent of the Financial Post, Mr. Clive Baxter, writing in that paper on December 10, goes further. He is writing from Brussels after having talks with officials of the European common market, and he has this to say, quoting an E.C.M. executive:
Please explain to Canadians that while we sympathize with your problems you cannot scare us with the sort of threats Mr. Fleming used.
If you don't like what we are doing you are, of course, free to take whatever measures your government sees fit. ..
Much as we like Canada and Canadians, don't ever think that a market of 17 million people can threaten us into changing our basic plans...
Please don't lose your sense of proportion. You are going to have to live with us in the future, and to withdraw into an angry protective shell can only mean more and worse trouble for your economy.

The Budget-Mr. O'Leary good opportunity for it now. With new developments in Washington, I suggest it would be a great thing if the Canadian government could take the initiative in realizing this opportunity.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that this particular budget does not recognize the seriousness of the problems we face. Our country will solve these problems, of course. We on this side have faith and confidence in the Canadian people and in the destiny of Canada; but we have no faith or no confidence in a government which is not giving leadership, steady and wise administration, and which has not played its full part in the solution of those problems.
Our worry is not about the Canadian people; our worry is about the government, and that worry is shared by an increasing number of Canadian people. We have no illusions about the complexities and difficulties of the problems. We know there is no single solution for our problems. In this respect, maybe I can quote with complete approval another paragraph from the speech of the governor of the Bank of Canada. He said the other day:
Our difficulties have a variety of causes, and some combination of a number of various lines of attack will no doubt provide the best solution. It is important to realize, however, that there is no single easy solution, no method which does not involve effort and thought and the adaptation of earlier ideas to the actual conditions of the day.
The lead in such effort and thought and in the adaptation of earlier ideas to the problems should be given by this government. That is not being done. That is why we moved this amendment, and that is why we will vote for it.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the Leader of the Opposition permit a question? Mine is a very simple mind, particularly with respect to finance. The Leader of the Opposition deplores federal deficits; he advocates cuts in taxation, in corporation and personal income tax. He advocates more spending. How does he reconcile these three?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would not try to reconcile what the hon. member has just said because I never advocated any such thing.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not undertake to comment at any length on the remarks just concluded by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). I will simply say I was deeply disappointed that he continued to parade that note of pessimism so characteristic of the party that he leads. I was also a bit amazed and surprised at the inconsistency obviously shown when he indicated certain agreement with the principles of this


budget and yet at the same time he continued to criticize the policies set forth in it.
On Tuesday evening the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) commented that this budget contained nothing for the Atlantic provinces. When I have concluded my remarks I believe I will have proved conclusively that this statement was inaccurate. I will refer to direct benefits that will accrue to my constituency from this budget, and I will also refer to indirect benefits, and I would ask the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo to put the two of them together and recognize the fact that these indirect benefits apply to us in the Atlantic provinces as Canadians. I must admit there were a number of years when I doubted whether Ottawa did recognize the Atlantic provinces as Canadian provinces. However, this government, in one of its first acts, very quickly dispelled any doubts that we had in our minds. I refer, of course, to the special grants of $25 million to the Atlantic provinces.
I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) first of all on having seen fit to introduce this supplementary budget at this time; and, second, on the nature and content of it. That it was timely was well expressed by the minister himself in his opening remarks when he said, as reported at page 999 of Hansard:
Not only must policies be flexible from year to year, but there are occasions when it becomes appropriate to reassess the economic outlook and to adjust fiscal policies between the main budget dates. This is such a time.
The recognition of the need for flexibility in our economic policies to which the minister referred both last month and on introducing this present interim budget is the reason we have this budget before us. I noted that on Monday my respected friend, the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) did not embrace too warmly the concept of flexibility that the minister pointed out; but I sincerely believe that this hon. member is the type of person who, if he were in the minister's position, would not permit changing economic conditions both at home and abroad to take place without taking what he would feel would be appropriate action as quickly as possible to cope with such a fast changing national economy. This is exactly what the Minister of Finance has done.
During my few years in this house I have gained the impression that the Liberal party on more than one occasion felt, or at least attempted to convey the idea, that this government did not act promptly enough or was too inflexible or did not adapt itself readily enough to change. Obviously the hon. member for Welland does not support this idea.

On Monday last the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bell) neatly summed up the objectives of this budget. He did this in five propositions and I feel they are well worth repeating here. I quote from page 1079 of Hansard:
To provide immediate stimulus to employment; to intensify the impetus to balanced economic development; to encourage more effective use of Canadian savings in the development of our resources and industry; to assist in the improvement of our balance of payments situation and to keep a tight rein on inflationary pressures.
So far in this debate I have not heard any of the opposition members provide anything by way of conviction that such objectives could not or would not be attained.
It is quite true, Mr. Speaker, that this supplementary budget, because of what it sets out to do in order to meet the challenge of the times, will mean a deficit at the end of the fiscal year rather than a modest surplus as predicted by the Minister of Finance last March. I ask, what is the reaction of the people of Canada to this deficit as forecast? I think it is obvious that they recognize it as a further indication of the Progressive Conservative party keeping faith with the people and, more specifically, with the Prime Minister's pledge to the effect that the welfare of Canadians would be a prime consideration, deficit or no deficit.
Certainly no one in this nation should be shocked by deficits as such and certainly not in this instance when the budget provides for these worthy objectives which I have already outlined. As has already been pointed out by speakers on the government side in this debate, deficits have been experienced many times in this country both under Liberal and Conservative administrations. Then too, it has been quite correctly pointed out that the present forecast deficit represents but 5.6 per cent of our total expenditures for this year whereas under Liberal administrations in the past we have had deficits representing 14.6, 19 and even as high as 35 per cent of the total expenditures in those days. These reflections should cushion the pretended shock of even the most pronounced opposition critics.
The tax and fiscal measures outlined in the budget plus the legislation already passed by the house during the pre-Christmas session provide for an increased program of assistance to municipalities for winter works projects; improvement in the terms of mortgage lending; Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in partnership with provincial authorities undertaking the purchase, improvement and rental of existing housing; loans to universities for students' residences; establishment of a productivity council; loans to 90205-6-81J
The Budget-Mr. O'Leary small businesses; generous assistance to provincial vocational training programs, plus a further 21 measures to come before the house, all this adds up, Mr. Speaker, to a program of such a nature and of such magnitude as should allay even the voiced fears of the gloomiest of opposition members.
Representing a constituency of farming, fishing and small businesses of various types and, incidentally, the seat of a university world renowned in the field of adult education, I know that the people of my area will quickly recognize and appreciate the several items in the government's program which directly apply. I will not labour the matter by reciting the entire field where these various measures directly apply, but considering the productive components of my constituency as I have already stated them it is obvious from which measures it will benefit most.
However, I do feel that I must make brief reference to the rural rehabilitation and development program referred to in both the throne and the budget speeches. In so far as my constituency is concerned, this legislation and the ensuing action will be warmly welcomed. I know this will be true right across the country, and I would point out that it is but one more of many progressive steps toward a well-rounded national agricultural policy as announced by the Prime Minister on August 30, 1958. I wish to quote briefly and in part the words of the Minister of Finance with reference to this item in his budget presentation on December 20, as found at page 1003 of Hansard. With reference to the rehabilitation and development program, he said:
This measure envisages a far-reaching program of rural development which taken together with existing facilities and program for assistance to farmers adds up to a well rounded and comprehensive agricultural policy for Canada. Under this program, to be undertaken in co-operation with the provinces, we may look forward to a general betterment in the quality of our agricultural resources through projects for soil improvement and water conservation; the diversification of economic opportunities available in rural areas; the more effective use of marginal lands by converting them to community pastures and woodlots. These and other related activities encompassed in this program are directed to the long standing objective of the government to raise the standard of living and improve the economic opportunities of our rural population.
In view of the fact that at the present time a large section of our rural population is trying to make a living on marginal and submarginal land and that approximately one third of our farmers across Canada have a gross income of $1,200 a year or less, the need of such a program goes unquestioned. Incidentally, in the province of Nova Scotia and in my constituency the number who have

The Budget-Mr. O'Leary a gross income of $1,200 or less considerably exceeds one third of the total number.
I know that the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan), the constituency adjoining mine on the east, will agree with me that this measure is timely indeed. I refer to the $40 million pulp mill being constructed in his constituency directly across the strait of Canso from Guysborough county and which it is planned will be in operation in the first quarter of 1962. Both our constituencies can provide ample scope for the conversion of marginal and submarginal land into specialized use for forest crops and thereby provide an additional source of wood supply for this new mill.
In addition, of course, to the forestry aspect of this legislation, we hope that there will be embraced such other urgent matters as farm surpluses, more productive use of our land and water resources, drainage, erosion control and the establishment of many of our farmers on economic family farm units. I believe the hope of this legislation is to provide new and diversified opportunities that are at present not available to traditional agriculture. Those farmers who have not classified as at least reasonably productive in the traditional field will be afforded an opportunity to move into other new and specialized fields, and those whose higher productivity warrants their remaining in traditional agriculture will as a result immediately increase their opportunities to pick up markets formerly supplied by an aggregate of these low productive farmers who have moved into other than traditional fields of agriculture. Thus we see that all farmers in all regions of Canada will benefit by this legislation.
The Nova Scotia federation of agriculture in its 1960 annual brief presented to the Nova Scotia members of the house recommended practically the identical solutions which we understand will be part and parcel of this rural rehabilitation and development legislation as outlined in the budget.
At this time, because it is directly related and is of vital concern to our farm woodlot owners, I wish to commend the government on its establishment of the Department of Forestry last year. I compliment the Prime Minister on his excellent selection of a minister to head this department. At the same time I warmly congratulate the minister on his appointment.
Like other members, I have received numerous inquiries for information with respect to the small business loans legislation and I was very pleased to hear the Minister of Finance say on Tuesday in replying to a question that the regulations and application forms had been distributed to the banks and it was expected that lending
IMr. O'Leary.]
operations would commence yesterday. I am pleased too and I know that all across Canada our university students and their parents welcomed the budget announcement with respect to the allowance of tuition fees before calculating taxable income where applicable.
When listing the items of legislation enacted during the pre-Christmas session I included loans to universities for students' residences.
I do not think I need remind the house that such a measure is much appreciated by almost all Canadian universities so hard pressed to accommodate their ever-growing student bodies. Unprecedented numbers of students are entering our universities. As a matter of fact, the annual increase in enrolment since 1955 has considerably outpaced the forecast of the statisticians. This would lead one to believe that even though the granting of scholarships offer desirable opportunities to Canadians and therefore have genuine merit the great problem in this field today is the plight of our universities in attempting to provide facilities and accommodation for the increasing numbers of our young people who presently have or may secure the funds with which to attend university and who cannot be accommodated.
The Canadian Universities Foundation made this very clear when presenting its brief to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in October, 1960. This brief states in part, and I quote:
Scholarships to aid the individual are good in part, but it must be remembered that a scholarship, like a cheque, is valuable only if the institutions possess the assets to back it up.
The brief goes on to say, and I quote:
The present preoccupation of the universities is to find sufficient funds to look after unprecedented numbers of students.
Obviously the Liberal party, in its recent pronouncements outside of this house, almost wholly ignored this important fact. It is true that in their resolution on this subject they did indicate that present federal grants for the support of universities would be continued and extended as necessary. I wonder, however, if they would not have exemplified a greater grasp of the problem if they had included something more akin to this government's recent action in introducing the loans to universities legislation.
Appreciating this splendid legislation, never forgetting to be grateful to this government for being the first administration to tangibly recognize the special needs of the Atlantic provinces by making available to them some $25 million annually; not losing sight of the fact that this government since taking office has increased direct assistance to universities by 20 per cent of the total grants made between 1952 and 1957 or paid 60 per cent

of the total grants made between 1952 and 1960; not overlooking the fact that in 1958 this government increased per capita grants to universities from $1 to $1.50, I now call to the attention of the Minister of Finance the unique and unfortunate position of Nova Scotia universities with respect to these per capita grants. I would point out immediately that the formula for these grants was not set up by this government but rather by the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences in 1952. I know that the minister is already aware of this situation and would welcome an immediate solution.
Simply stated, the problem results from the fact that all the universities of Nova Scotia draw their students from outside the province to a greater extent than universities in the other nine provinces. For example, the rates of student population to total population in the university year 1959-60 was 1 to 136. By contrast, the rate for Newfoundland was 1 to 424. In terms of dollars received, this meant that for 1959-60 Nova Scotia universities received $203 per student or $432 per student less than Newfoundland. This amount was $63 less per student than the average grant per student for all Canada which was $271. I realize that comparing the per student grant for the province of Newfoundland is scarcely fair in view of the circumstances. However, I do so only because Newfoundland receives the highest per student grant of any of the provinces. The case I wish to make here is that Nova Scotia university grants should immediately be brought up to the national average, if at all possible.
If Nova Scotia universities had received grants equal to the national average they would have received an additional $359,312 in the academic year 1959-60 alone. St. Francis Xavier University at Antigonish would have received approximately $100,000 more for that year alone. Recognizing the great need for steadily increasing operating income for all universities, as is illustrated by Edward Sheffield in the publication entitled "Financial Needs of Canadian Universities", it is not difficult to understand why the position of Nova Scotia universities particularly is becoming precarious.
