subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will send the hon. member a copy of Hansard tomorrow, and he can look for it himself.
If Nova Scotia universities had received a grant equal to the national average, as I have already pointed out, they would have received $359,312 for the academic year 1959-60. Lest there be any misunderstanding of my argument for Nova Scotia universities by hon. members from British Columbia, Manitoba and New Brunswick, the other provinces where the per student grants to universities fall below the national average, I believe it best to quote from the Canadian Universities Foundation brief of October, 1960, in which it was noted that Nova Scotia constituted a special case. Arguments were advanced as to why this was so. Appendix C was added to this brief entitled "The Nova Scotia Universities: A special case". I will quote briefly the appropriate extracts from both the brief and appendix C. On page 12 of the brief, we find the following, and I should like to emphasize that this is not a Nova Scotia brief but the Canadian Universities Foundation brief:
We would like to emphasize here the point that Nova Scotia constitutes a special case, and that the problems in that province would not be solved even by the increase in per capita grants that we recommend. Dalhousie University, for instance, is responsible for a large part of both the professional and the graduate education, not only in Nova Scotia but in all the maritime provinces. All the universities of Nova Scotia draw their students from outside the province to a greater extent than universities elsewhere.
Then, on the same page the brief continues:
For this unusually large student population- the largest proportionate to provincial population of any section of Canada-there exist resources substantially lower than in any other area of Canada.
Then going to appendix C of this brief, page 1, we read:
-because this province has a large number of universities for its size and consequently a larger number of students in proportion to its population than the other provinces, its universities are inadvertently being penalized under the present system of federal grants in receiving a smaller grant per student than those of any other province.
Nova Scotia differs from the other provinces that also receive federal grants per student below the national average in that all of its universities are private foundations, except a provincial technical college which provides only the last two years of the engineering course. They are not therefore in receipt of the very extensive provincial support accorded to the provincially-oper-ated universities by other provinces and extended to their private universities as well. Moreover, the very existence of the larger proportion of students in relation to provincial population in

The Budget-Mr. O'Leary Nova Scotia would make such an undertaking more onerous than in the higher income provinces of central and western Canada.
On page 2 we find the following:
Not only are the Nova Scotian universities hampered in cultivating the province's most precious resource-its people-they are, in educating many young people from other provinces and many young Nova Scotians who move to other parts of the country, trying to discharge a national responsibility under a severe financial handicap. The national outlook and function of Canadian universities, referred to earlier in this submission, is no less characteristic of Nova Scotian universities than of those of other provinces. Indeed, the relatively greater pressure of increased enrolment in central and western Canada is bound to induce more and more students from other provinces to enter Nova Scotian universities and thus to enhance their national character. Here then is an added reason for assuring the universities of this province of adequate support.
Then on page 3:
It has been pointed out that even though the need for federal financial support has, if anything, been greater in Nova Scotia than in the wealthier provinces, the federal grants to Nova Scotia per student have been, since their inception, not only below the national average, but the lowest received by any of the provinces.
Then in its conclusion the appendix states:
Only extraordinary financial assistance can save Nova Scotia's universities from severe deterioration in the next few years.
I fully realize, Mr. Speaker, that this whole subject of per capita grants to universities is an integral part of federal-provincial agreements and I have no doubt that under the new agreements of 1962 a more equitable formula will be set up. However, in view of the emphasis which the Canadian Universities Foundation, voicing the sentiments of the majority of our universities across Canada, has given the subject of Nova Scotia universities with respect to these grants, I hope that the Minister of Finance and this government may see fit to offer some alleviation of the problem at the earliest opportunity.
I stated earlier, Mr. Speaker, that I would not recite in detail all of the measures in this budget which directly affect and offer assistance and relief for the people in my constituency, the people of Nova Scotia and the people of the Atlantic provinces. I have mentioned but a few of those direct benefits. I will now conclude by way of a general statement indicating that those measures to which I have not referred, those measures which indirectly affect not only my constituency but my province and Canada as a whole, are but further positive proof of this government's genuine concern for the people of Canada, for Canadian ownership and control of our country's resources and industries, for expanded productivity and full employment and its determination and ability to carry out its pledges to the electorate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to congratulate the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for the masterful speech he just made in this house. I know that others among my follow members will have the opportunity to air their views and say whether they consider the opposition leader's allegations justified.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, before coming to the point of the matter-I say to the point of the matter, because some of my friends will find in it matters that are rather pointed-I would like to rectify a statement made this morning by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker), when he asked in this house why we, the Liberals, were not bringing up that famous question of national census, which has aroused so much protest. First of all, Mr. Speaker, it is not because the Prime Minister mentioned the matter that I am dealing with it. I might say to the Prime Minister that if he had taken the trouble of reading the official record or if some of his friends had done so, he would have found that the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine) did refer to the matter of the census and expressed some very clear and concise views on the subject. He was one of two Liberals in the house who dealt with the matter. His share was 50 per cent, whereas on the Conservative side, the percentage is zero. Mr. Speaker, this is the proportion of those in the two great parties who are discharging their responsibilities in the house, and that is not all.
I now come to what I shall call "the Pigeon incident." When the Leader of the Opposition was speaking a moment ago, an hon. member rose and said: "Tell us about Mr. St. Laurent and his view." I am delighted that my good friend should like to hear our views on Mr. St. Laurent's statement. He will realize that inside the Liberal party, we are free to express our opinion.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I shall say that I, for my part, am proud of my ethnic origin. That ethnic origin is French and I am proud of it. I owe it to my ancestors, while for my Canadian nationality, of which I am also proud, I am indebted to Mr. St. Laurent, the former Liberal prime minister, who caused that origin to be recognized in this house.
Now, since our friends are anxious to hear about Mr. St. Laurent, may I say this: When Mr. St. Laurent was prime minister of Canada he assumed his responsibilities.

When, in 1961, he gives his personal opinion as a citizen of the province of Quebec, I respect that opinion to which he is entitled. But I would point out to my friends opposite that if Mr. St. Laurent assumed his responsibilities when he was prime minister, the present Prime Minister should also assume his. And the outcry arising from various parts of this country at the moment is directed against the head of the present government and the arbitrary decisions taken by his government, and he is the one who must assume any responsibility, so long as he remains the head of the government.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, with reference to Mr. St. Laurent, I should like to compare the 1951 census taken under Mr. St. Laurent to the coming 1961 census. Mr. St. Laurent's government, like all former governments, always respected ethnic origin. Question 17 in the 1951 census read as follows:
What Is your origin?
In answer to that you have:
English, French, Irish, and so on.
How can our Conservative friends from Quebec remain complacent or at least silent while the 1961 census, under their administration, is about to do away with ethnic origin completely and while such data is essential if the census is to have any historical significance?
Mr. Speaker, I am definitely against this item which has been introduced into the 1961 census form, item No. 10 which says:
What is your origin on your father's side?
The first answer suggested to that question is "Canadian origin".
Mr. Speaker, my own ethnic origin is French, and I am proud of it. At the same time, I know that people whose ethnic origin is other than mine are also proud of theirs. If anyone anywhere is ashamed to say that he comes from Germany, or elsewhere, let him use, as was indicated on the 1951 census form, the last square of question No. 17.
Did you know, that in the 1951 form, a special clause or space was provided for anyone ashamed to say that he came from Germany or elsewhere.
Mr. Speaker, this concludes my remarks on the census. I am anxious however to see our friends opposite assume their responsibilities.
As for Mr. St. Laurent, I shall be forever grateful to him for giving Canadian citizenship to Canada, and I shall keep calling him
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis a great Canadian. I respect his personal views, knowing that he respects ours.
I shall now deal with the speech delivered on television the day before yesterday by the Prime Minister of Canada. Yesterday's issue of La Presse reported that speech as follows. The Prime Minister stated:
The Progressive Conservative government has been criticized for its inability to provide an answer to the unemployment problem since it came into power three and a half years ago. But far from being a new problem, unemployment had been a chronic uneasiness, affecting the Canadian economy for a long time. Because those things were not done when they should have been, the entire Canadian economy found itself defenceless against the foreseeable effects of the recession that was already in progress when we came into power in June 1957.
I like it very much when the Prime Minister says he was defenceless against the effects that were nevertheless foreseeable. Therefore he did foresee the effects he mentioned. If he did foresee those alleged effects, why then did he proclaim throughout Canada during his 1957 and 1958 election campaigns:
(Text) :
"No one will suffer as long as I am Prime Minister".

Why did he state to the whole country that he, John Diefenbaker, was able to settle all those problems in no time?

Mr. Bennett, prime minister of Canada, stated on March 17, 1931, that is, a few months after he came to power in this country-you will think, Mr. Speaker, that it was the present prime minister speaking. This is what Mr. Bennett said in 1931:
Why is it that present conditions prevail in Canada? Do you realize that if this country had been making thoughtful provision for the future, if its leaders had been looking into the future, with eyes of vision, there should not have come this disaster to the Canadian people?
And Mr. Bennett added:
Do you realize that this government has been in power eight months and that whatever conditions prevail in Canada today are attributable, not to it but to the governments that preceded it?
Mr. Speaker, the more we compare Mr. Bennett's words with those of Mr. Diefen-baker, the more we realize that they are similar, to the point of completely merging together.
Mr. Speaker, here is another gem spoken by Mr. Bennett, who was still prime minister, but by then he had been in power five years, since the statement is dated 1935. Four years had elapsed since the first and the second statement. In the first instance, after eight months in power he had said: "Blame that on the others, and give me time."
The following statement was made four years later. In January 1935 the same R. B. Bennett shortly before his notorious downfall said this:
Is there one hon. member opposite who is so unfair as to ignore the circumstances under which we found ourselves In 1930?

The laments of the 1935 prime minister, we find them again in the mouth of the present Prime Minister, and in the words he spoke on television. The 1935 prime minister said: "We have been in power for only four and a half years and if things are not so good, others are to blame".

If we are elected, we will undertake and complete the St. Lawrence seaway.

This is a young country and there is no reason why there should be unemployment in the country, if the government knows its business.

There was no need to call a conference to settle the unemployment problem; the solution to the problem is quite obvious. Is it work you want instead of conferences? You are going to get itl I do not want to get into power at the cost of broken promises.

Under the circumstances and in view of the demagogy used once again by the Liberals, I find it enlightening that the Leader of the Opposition did not dare to assume his responsibilities and tell the Canadian population clearly what he, as leader of the Liberal party and Leader of the Opposition thinks of that census problem which is being dramatized.
I think this is an important problem. And if I have chosen to deal with it today in connection with the budget, it is because I meant to express my opinion on the matter.
The problem is an administrative one, which is both technical and scientific in nature. It is too bad that some people had to drag politics into it for reasons that are quite obvious from a partisan viewpoint.
Organizations for the preservation of French culture in Canada and a number of other societies for the promotion and defence of French culture in America have made representations to the government in an effort to have question 10 changed.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to repeat what I said on another occasion on this matter. I told a newspaperman in reply to his questions that I was willing to work with French organizations and to do everything in my power to bring about the changes desired by those organizations.
I carefully studied the many suggestions made, one of which recommends that the term "Canadian" be stricken from the census form.
According to newspaper reports, that would still appear to be the opinion and desire of those French organizations. As far as I am concerned, I think that if that solution was to be reached, I should accept it, but in my opinion it would not solve the problem completely, because the whole census form, as pointed out by a newspaperman in the morning issue of Le Devoir, is wrong from a demographic viewpoint, since it leads to no conclusion of any scientific value.
I think that a special commission made up of capable demographers and statisticians should be set up for the purpose of reconsidering the whole problem from the start,

reviewing all the census forms and reaching rational conclusions, so that proper authorities would get suggestions that would give the Canadian decennial census an unquestionable scientific value.
Mr. Speaker, having worked for many years among French organizations I know how important that census problem is to them. I know that they want the census clearly to show the extent of French culture in Canada. They want the census to determine the total number of the French Canadian group. They also want this census to show the trend in the development of the French Canadian group. I for one am willing to do everything possible so that their request is met and the census give the very results they expect.
Mr. Speaker, before passing to another subject, I should like once again to express my regrets of the fact that even in this house an attempt has been made to mess up that vital and important subject. I should like to express my regret, Mr. Speaker, of the fact that attempts are being made to play politics with this important question, and I deplore even more the fact that some people are taking this opportunity to criticize the intentions of the Conservative government, criitcism which can only result, Mr. Chairman, in impeding the national unity which we are striving for.

A moment ago, the census was mentioned and forgive me for coming back to it, it was said that if the Conservative government were to accept certain proposals it would eventually amount to a retreat.
Mr. Speaker, should the Conservative government accept the proposals put forward by French-Canadian associations, not only would it not retreat but it would once again show the people that it is a democratic government, a government of the people for the people, a government which has been able once more to take into consideration the representations made to it. A democratic government, Mr. Speaker, is elected by the people and as such must take the wishes of the people into consideration. In accepting the proposals submitted to it by its citizens, the government does nothing but show that it respects our democratic institutions and that it intends for them to be respected.
Whatever they say or do, our colleagues from the Liberal party will never succeed in making the least change in the policies they have advocated and which repeat word for word the ones put before the nation in 1958 by the Leader of the Opposition. That program was rejected by the nation in a resounding way and that is why we on this side are here in such great numbers.

I feel, Mr. Speaker, that a political party is a free association of free men. I have always been free in my party to say what I wanted to. And if today, I took the liberty to say openly what I felt about that question of the census, it was because I knew that no one in my party, not even the Prime Minister, would blame me. However I have noticed how a member of the Liberal party had humiliated the former prime minister of Canada by rejecting-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because this debate permits a rather unusual latitude, I had hoped to use most of the half hour to make some comments on the official opposition, the Liberal party, its leader, and the party image, real or fancied. Unfortunately, I outsmarted myself in finding a spot on the debate roster, and I have not enough time to do the job properly. I can only promise the members I shall try to carry on later and complete the job at a proper time in the house.
First, however, I should like to note that a previous member for Port Arthur, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, died as last year ended. The normal eulogies and services have taken place, and perhaps it may seem superfluous or impertinent for me to comment now. However, C. D., as he was known in Port Arthur and beyond, was, and perhaps justifiably so, considered the greatest person our community has put on the Canadian public stage. I say "perhaps", not niggling, because another former M.P., for our area, who has tended to be very much admired by many people, was a great Canadian and was also an engineer. I refer to Mr. S. J. Dawson who built the famous Dawson trail westward and opened up the west in a way that set a tradition for Mr. Howe. In any case, the name of Dawson appears in Canadian history books as a pioneer developer. I think it likely that Mr. Howe's name will also do so.
If that seems over-cautious, you should check your history text and find out little attention has been paid to other great nation builders of the past. One might hazard that Mr. Howe's place in history books a half century from now will be secured by two things, namely his role in the political controversy of the pipe line debate and the subsequent electoral upheaval and by his creation of quasi-socialistic entities such as T.C.A. and Polymer Corporation. There may be an irony and a lesson in this because C. D. was thought of as a rugged individualist rather than a creeping socialist and also because the incidents that destroy an administration linger longer in memory than do its achievements.
The Budget-Mr. Fisher
By most people in the lakehead Mr. Howe was immensely respected, although I think it would be a fair generalization to say that he was not generally beloved. His integrity as a powerful minister in relation to his community was a model. There were never stories of graft or personal interference in the handing out of jobs as far as Mr. Howe was concerned. Mr. Howe was a grand loser as a politician defeated in his own constituency. I met him a few minutes after he had conceded defeat. His manner was brusque, but not because he was downcast or hurt but because he was already restless to get on to something else. His comment to me was "Young man, young man, there are so many things I want to do; we're really going to enjoy ourselves". I think he meant by that he and his wife. One felt that the whole future was ahead of him.
That aspect of purposefulness, the refusal to be petty or morose were fine characteristics of Port Arthur's most famous citizen. His memory as a member and as a man will last there for a long long time. The historians and the economists will in time set out his national significance. I felt it incumbent upon me, with respect to this famous member for Port Arthur, to give that analysis and to pay that tribute.
The second topic I wish to touch on briefly relates to my constituency, the pre-Christmas legislative program and the baby budget. In an area where unemployment is high, there was interest and approval for several items enacted, particularly loans to small businesses, the vocational training program and the subsidies for municipal sewage projects. I found in the recess that this approval was tentative because the effectiveness remains to be seen. The budget has made little impact of a positive kind, in my opinion, because it has so little direct bearing on the average taxpayer personally. In a sense it seems to have been taken by my constituents as a mysterious exercise in monetary and fiscal policy which will be judged not even on results but on what more concrete steps may be taken in the spring regular budget.
The third point upon which I wish to touch relates to the census of 1961 which has developed somewhat of an issue, as witness the motion unanimously adopted in the Quebec provincial legislature protesting the federal government's acceptance of the word "Canadian" as an answer to a census question on ethnic origin. The assembly is to

The Budget-Mr. Fisher forward a message to Ottawa asking that "Canadian" and "American" be deleted from the printed list of possible ethnic origins on the next census forms.
We will hope that some accommodation can be made to French-Canadian wishes to have statistical information on their particular language and cultural group. However, I hope the government appreciates the fact that many Canadians think of themselves as Canadians rather than as members of some ethnic group of hyphenated Canadian. In my own case, I happen to be a fifth generation Canadian. Probably my paternal ancestors came from England but if you came to figure out my ethnic nationality, what is it? What about the Irish, Scotch, Pennsylvania Dutch or any of these others that entered the strain? I would have a hard time in detei-mining it.
To take my own constituency as an example, I may say that it is a real swirl of national backgrounds if you were going to carry the matter back and examine each citizen's antecedents. In one class a few years ago I happened to make this check. I had children whose paternal line apparently or actually-apparently as far as they knew -was linked with Ukrainia, Finland, Poland, Italy, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Hungary, Serbia, Macedonia, France, Russia and the British Isles. What were they, even for statistical purposes or any other real purpose, but Canadians? I believe it is right that people like that should have the right to consider themselves as Canadians, simply as Canadians to declare or to register as such. I hope that point of view can be confirmed in the arrangement or in the change that may be made in order to accommodate this kind of protest that has come from the province of Quebec.
It is not in the same way that the governor of Alabama said, "Some of my best friends are niggers", that I say that some of my best friends are Liberals. It is not in that way at all. I was brought up in a Liberal family; I have voted for Liberal candidates; I have run errands as a boy for Liberals during elections; and I am sure some of my closest relations still vote Liberal. I took a full year at university studying Liberalism in its Canadian context. The biggest files I have in my filing cabinet relate to Liberalism and the Liberal party. It is with that intense interest that I should like to move on to an analysis of the Liberal party, especially in the light of the rally it has just had.


The Liberal party has not had too many rallies but I would suggest to the majority of the members of the house who are Conservative that they should go back and take a look at the previous records of such rallies which took place in 1893, 1918, 1948. There was a smaller convocation in 1943 that might be considered a rally and there was one in 1958. I think the Liberal rally of 1961 was a most important political event. I do not downgrade it at all. Political rallies are going to become more and more important in our democratic process. I think one of the reasons -and I will say this offhand-is that people notice their circus aspects possibly more than they do the traditional development of party position each day in the House of Commons.
This rally was an important event. It would seem to have confirmed the party leadership and made partial steps at least to a new party platform. One of the things it did was the bringing of several thousand Liberals from across the country to engage in open discussion. A sizeable achievement. I cannot comprehend the pundits amongst the Liberals or the press who have said they felt there were some risks in these open discussions. Surely the process of democracy is always risky, being in the open, but that is what the party should be doing, namely democratically discussing things out in the open. I would be shocked if at the convention that our group is going to enter into this August the discussions of policy were not out in the open. I would be surprised if the Conservative party rally in March holds its discussions in secret. It seems to me that the rally, in this sense of bringing people together for the exchange of ideas was a success for the Liberals and should be so recognized. I am delighted, of course, that it means that their organization is going to be strong and they are going to be able to go out to the hustings with a better organization and bags of money. I was elected in a good tight three-way fight and I think most members will be elected in the coming election in a three-way fight. We want the Liberals to have some strength for such battles.
At this point I should like to ask this question. What have the Liberals? They are a party that has a tradition of power in the country. A great many families pass it on from father to son. These loyalties endure for a time. That is one of the reasons why they will continue to have across the country a modicum of support. That support is no longer as important as it was, but it is important.
They have a great deal of strength in the province of Quebec, and it is very apparent

from the Liberal administration there now that Quebec is still in that tradition which dates back to Riel, was buttressed by the conscription issue in the first world war and follows on to the present day. So many members of the Liberal party in this house are from Quebec, a further indication of continuing strength there.
Another source of Liberal strength, in our part of the country at least, is among those immigrants who came into Canada from 1896 to the first world war, and their descendants -I do not mean the French Canadian-and these immigrant groups, were exclusively Liberal or have so continued, but these, plus those Irish-Catholic grouping have kept the Liberal tradition very strong. Their thinking and feeling-except for those who may have become radicals-is perhaps the greatest Liberal asset. Another is that, until recently it has been the party in power and there is the fresh memory of jobs, emoluments and money that have been handed out. Many of the lawyers in our community are still staunchly Liberal, still hoping, I think that they will be handling C.M.H.C. mortgages again, will be considered for judgeships, and so on.
I know many of the intellectuals, the academic people in the universities fairly well. Many of them are continuing Liberals because they were consulted and had jobs from the Liberals, a practice so well-instituted by Mackenzie King.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-13, to amend the Canada Elections Act, (publication of straw poll results).
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is not new; it has been discussed in the house over a period of time. Its purpose is to prevent the publication of the results of straw polls conducted after the issuance of a writ for an election. Some provinces, notably British Columbia, for many years have had on their statutes legislation which prohibits the publication of the results of straw polls. British Columbia has found that this has produced no hardship and has left the people of that province free from the erroneous results which sometimes flow from opinion polls conducted to ascertain what the wishes of the people are going to be at election time.
One of the good things that flow from polls conducted for election purposes is that eventually the people themselves do have some say as to whether the poll is right or not and they do settle this problem. It is unlike some of the results of opinion polls which are conducted in the commercial sphere, where people never have the opportunity of deciding whether they as the majority wanted whatever the opinion poll suggested they wanted and got. While there is this final answer, the answer that will be given on election day, it seems to me that for a number of reasons the influences that are afforded by various media of publication can be misdirected during an election period.
The main discussions that have taken place in this country and in other countries in recent years concern the election between Mr. Dewey and Mr. Truman in which all the opinion polls, not only the opinion polls as we hold them in Canada but polls that were conducted among various news commentators, radio people, television commentators and others, indicated overwhelmingly the election of Mr. Dewey. Since that time a great deal of study has taken place into why the results of the opinion pollsters-all of them, of course supporting Mr. Dewey-should have been so overwhelmingly in error, and why those opinion pollsters should have been taken in by the pseudo scientific polls that took place.
When we had this bill before us the last time I was very interested in the discussion by members of the government and their defence of the newspaper industry and why they considered this to be placing a limit on the freedom of the press. Since that time I have taken upon myself the duty of examining into how opinion polls are formed. I have

read some of the discussions that have taken place between pollsters and commentators with respect to the disreputable position in which they found themselves by having put forth pseudo scientific information which they later found to be no real information at all.
If any hon. member wishes to read the explanatory notes of the bill he will see that some of the things I was accused of wanting to accomplish by the introduction of this bill were just not so at all. I have no objection to the taking of polls on elections because, as I have said, the final decision rests with the voters, and we can check the pseudo scientific examination made by the pollsters against the actual record that is available after the election has taken place. Therefore, we have no objection to the polls being conducted, but we do have objection to the results of those polls being published.
This raises the question of why we should be opposed to anything which indicates that the voters are all going to vote for one particular party, or 41 per cent of the voters are going to vote one way and 43 per cent another way, and 16 per cent are going to vote in a still different way. Why should we object to this? I hasten to suggest that we have no objection to this; but if we are to form an opinion on opinion polls and the results of those polls, then we must ascertain for ourselves-and the press has an obligation to assess for us the honesty and the integrity of the people taking the polls-how accurate those polls are. When we are told that the people are going to vote one particular way, then we should be told how the pollsters know they are going to vote that way, what questions were asked, how much of the general public was sampled, in what areas the sampling took place, how general it was and what was the multiplication factor that applied to all the people of Canada, or to whatever country the polls happened to be taken in.
In the recent election in the United States- and it is too recent for us to find out what was the actual error in the so-called scientific polls-according to some of the articles I read, there was a difference of opinion, or an indication of a difference of opinion, among the voters of over 3 per cent.
As we know, in the recent election in the United States there was a difference of much less than 1 per cent in the results of the vote. Therefore, it is quite possible, although I am not suggesting this was the case, that those voters represented by the over 3 per cent could have been influenced when it came to casting their votes in the United States election.
I have here volume 80 of American Mercury for 1955 and I should like to refer to

an interesting article on page 134 by Joan Tara. It is headed "Can You Trust Opinion Research Polls?" She gives some consideration to this matter. She points out that opinion pollsters are always highly educated and that she and most of her fellow workers were educated in the academic sense. She herself has a bachelor of arts degree and I believe that of all those whom she knew only one had specialized in statistics. She says that she studied under a professor who scarcely knew what he was talking about and consequently she says that she knows even less. She goes on to say:
I suppose you are curious to learn the inner workings of a poll. It is a very curious business. The most spectacular polls are of a political nature. What percentage of the adult American population wants to throw brickbats at Senator Bosh this week as compared to last week? How many farmers favour the price of putty in New Zealand as compared to the price of coals in Newcastle? These are the opinion findings that make front page (second section of your newspaper) headlines.
Then she goes on to talk about the bread and butter polls in industry. She points out some very interesting facts. I do not want to read everything she says but if anybody is interested I would recommend that he read this article. On page 135 she goes on to say:
How does the pollster go about prying the answers loose from the great American public? First of all, he and his hired experts hammer out the list of questions which they believe will best elicit the required information. Armed with these preliminary questionnaires, the experts approach the man in the street. Sometimes the client prefers or needs, instead, the opinion of the man behind the plow, the man in the factory, or the man who owns a $15,000 ranch type house in the suburbs. If so, the experts get 100 questionnaires answered. This is called a sampling. From this sampling flows all the rest.
This is the interesting part as to how they arrive at the sample.
Back in the office, with its imposing views of the New York harbour, east and west, the experts study the questionnaires, smooth out the kinds, clarify questions that are too vague, misleading or unprofitable information-wise. They then compose a list of questions as near ideal as possible. Meanwhile, the official statisticians break down the answers from the sampling into categories, and the categories into percentages based on 100.
She uses an example of polls with regard to commercial activities and points out that once these are made the real pollsters go to work. They go out and ask questions of people across the country in more or less minute numbers and these samplings are returned to the office. On the wall before them always is the indication of the answers of 100 American people, so many having answered this way and so many that way and no matter how vague the answer appears to be it must fit into that pattern. When they
Canada Elections Act
arrive at the total, those that do not fit into that pattern are considered to be too vague to be of any importance to the poll and are discarded.
It is her contention that when the results of the poll are arrived at they are never more than 1 or 2 per cent out from the original sample because they have been tailored to fit into the sample which is always before the people who are compiling the statistics. She points out that the people compiling the statistics are also well educated in the same way she was and therefore she places no reliance on the results of these polls. She ends her article by saying:
It is time the nation's economic mills cease to depend upon largely imaginary figures to tell it what and what not to produce. It's time to put quality ahead of quantity. Either you have faith in your ability to produce the best possible mousetrap, faith in your own integrity to give the best you are capable of creating to the public, or you are cheating. Statistics mean nothing.
These words, of course, can easily be applied to politics and it is here that we do not agree with many of the people who spoke against the bill the last time it was before the house. We believe in the integrity and the intelligence of the man in the street. We know that if he is given the opportunity to decide for himself he will make a decision according to his own likes and as he sees the question. We think this is the way it should be done.
In the last year or so reference has been made in the House of Commons to an instance where the head of one of the largest polls in Canada was also engaged in other activities and was the head of another organization which certainly allowed no opinion to be expressed but decided itself what the view of the public should be on the matter. I refer, of course, to the trading stamp issue that came before parliament in several forms last year. These are the type of people whose integrity has already been questioned and is doubtful, people who are mainly concerned with such things as selling automobiles, ties, new hats and other things of a commercial nature.
I think that the people of Canada are entitled not to be confused as they are in the commercial field by high pressure gimmicks of one type or another used by high pressure pollsters but rather are entitled to all the facts and to make their own decision on those facts. I suggest that many occasions will arise, as happened in the United States particularly in the election contest between Truman and Dewey, when you will find a great deal of influence exerted. We will never know in that particular case how much influence was exerted by the newspapers through their adherence to polls of various kinds and the

Canada Elections Act
views of commentators who conducted other polls of a different nature. We will never know how much influence that had on the people and what the results of that election might otherwise have been.
All we are suggesting is that we do as British Columbia has done with no particularly bad effects, prohibit the publication of the results of these polls prior to election day so that the people themselves can vote with all the facts before them and without undue influence being exerted on them through being told that 1,217,000 people are going to vote for John Doe's party on election day and so many other people are going to vote for somebody else.
It is impossible for these pollsters to say this, Mr. Speaker. They never at any time take a poll of that number of people. They are estimating that according to the sampling they have taken this is the number of people who may vote in a certain way and their estimate is based on the questions they have put to these people. They are giving the people a false impression. They do not say how many people have been questioned. They are saying that this is the percentage of the whole. They may have sampled only a very minute part of the whole.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be advantageous to the freedom of the press if they curtailed their activities in this field. If they use the Gallup, or other national polls, then by all means they should tell the people after the election, we conducted a poll at such and such a time and this was the result. This was the question asked and this was the result as we projected it into the national total. This is the indication that we received. If they do this, and if their statement proves to be relatively correct, then I think they will reap benefits in the future from any predictions they may make in other fields. I believe if this course was followed the public will give much more consideration to these polls than they are going to give if mistakes of the nature to which I have referred are allowed to continue.
In closing, I should say that I believe the Canadian people are democratic enough, are smart enough and have the integrity to assess all the facts, without the necessity of pollsters giving them false impressions. The people are able to assess the facts and make their own decision without undue pressure from these statisticians.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday we had before us what was described as a perennial bill. Although it did not come to a vote because of the number of members who wished to speak on it, the bill had a very commendable purpose, namely the limiting of interest. Today we have before us what could be described also as a perennial C.C.F. bill. The purpose of this bill is not so commendable, although its passage would also limit interest. Bill No. C-13 would limit interest in elections, and along with this limitation of interest it would also have the effect of reducing public information.
The mover of this bill made his purpose very clear. He said he wanted to make sure that people were not taken in by the public polls. He believes that the polls are taken to fit a certain pattern. High pressure pollsters was the way he described those who conduct these polls. He also makes his purpose, and I imagine it is the agreed purpose of the C.C.F. group of eight in this house, very clear in the wording of his bill. The bill reads in part as follows:
No person, company or corporation shall, in any province after the issue of the writ for an election, or after the dissolution of parliament or the occurrence of a vacancy in consequence of which a writ for an election is eventually issued, and before the hour of closing of the polls in such province, publish the result or purported result of a straw vote or poll of the political opinions of the electors or any of them in any electoral district or districts in Canada,-
He also makes his purpose even clearer in the explanatory note, which reads:
The purpose of this amendment is to prohibit, and to make punishable as an illegal practice, the publication in any manner before election day of the results of a straw vote or poll of the political opinions of the electors. The proposed amendment does not prohibit the taking of such a poll for private purposes.
Let us look at this explanatory note a little closer.
The purpose of this amendment is to prohibit, and to make punishable as an illegal practice, the publication in any manner before election day of the results of a straw vote or poll of the political opinions of the electors.
Then, there is the usual C.C.F. joker.
The proposed amendment does not prohibit the taking of such a poll for private purposes.

In other words, a political party can take its own straw vote and make use of it for its own private purposes. Coming from Saskatchewan and knowing the tremendous publicity organization of the C.C.F. out there,
I can see that party taking advantage of privately conducted polls and broadcasting favourable comments only all across the country. It would be a case of, we want to tell you only what we want you to know and only what is in our favour. I do not believe such high-handed information censorship is in keeping with our system of free expression of opinion in a free democracy.
I am sure that there are few in this house who would be party to instituting such a flagrant attempt at controlling press, radio and T.V. coverage during an election campaign.
I know the press, radio and T.V. of Canada can very well present their own defence against this attempt of at least some form of censorship, and they need no champion of their cause. However, as a former newspaperman I should like to make a few comments with regard to the freedom of the press, one of the main bulwarks of our way of life. I certainly do not agree with everything that appears in our press or everything that comes over our radio or T.V. In fact, I disagree most forcibly with many of the comments by the columnists. I do not agree, for instance, with the latest Gallup poll results because I have just returned from the prairies. I know from personal observation and personal contacts that the government's popularity in the west is much higher than the latest published poll would indicate.

I repeat, I find myself in disagreement with a lot of the writing from the press gallery and a lot of other newspaper stories. Perhaps I am a little closer to the actual facts than they are and know how the stories might better be written. Although I disagree with the latest Gallup poll results, I will not agree that these forms of expression of public opinion should be abolished.
We had this same attempt at censorship from the same member in 1959. The Hansard report of that debate makes interesting reading. On page 2897 of Hansard for April 21, 1959, the sponsor of this bill said:
For some odd reason, possibly a quirk of the Canadian mind, quite often our people have a tendency to accept these polls and decide that they have to vote in an election for the party that is going to win.
What a concept of the Canadian mind. What a concept of the Canadian people. In
Canada Elections Act
the opinion of the sponsor of this bill, the voters in our country cannot be trusted to make up their own minds and are waiting to be spoonfed with someone else's opinions before they can cast their votes. I do not think the Canadian people will welcome this assessment of their intelligence and common sense.
Public opinion polls are part of our election campaigns. These polls are conducted in other countries, that is to say in other free countries. They are not conducted in the U.S.S.R. or in soviet dominated satellites. Communist leaders will not tolerate such expressions of public opinion there.
Another interesting suggestion arises from the statement of this bill's sponsor that a Gallup poll might cause the Canadian people to decide they have to vote in an election for the party that is going to win. Coupled with this remark the move to prevent publications of Gallup polls is an admission that the sponsor's party is not going to win. This, it would appear, is the main reason for the bill before us.
I referred earlier to the freedom of the press. On other occasions in this house I have referred to this freedom which, as we all know, carries with it responsibilities of fair and accurate reporting. I do not need to elaborate on this matter because these facts were all brought out during the debate on the bill of rights.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I am opposed to this bill. I am opposed to the expressed purpose as stated by the sponsor.
I would hope that this bill would come to a vote because I want to vote against it. I know, however, that others will wish to express their opinions and I am sure the whole hour will be taken up in these expressions of views.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every year the socialists keep bringing in this bill to prohibit the sampling of public opinion just before elections and I can never understand why they do so. This is legislation against freedom of speech and freedom of the printed word. It is a direct contravening of the bill of rights. If a government banned the printing of election polls, would the next step be the banning of opinions of editorial writers or columnists or by radio and television commentators?
I suppose a time comes to all of us in public life when we do not like what the polls tell us. We look upon polls then with scorn because the opinion disclosed is not our opinion. The time has certainly come many times when the C.C.F. party has had a right to be scornful about polls on that basis, but that is certainly no reason to legislate against

Canada Elections Act
them. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) is insulting the Canadian people every time he brings this bill before the house. He is in effect saying that the Canadian people have no individual convictions and that they follow the majority blindly. He is saying that the Canadian people are a lot of sheep. He is exposing a personal superiority over the elector that does not become him.
Public opinion polls have been functioning around this world for 25 years and I think we would be a laughing stock in Britain, France and India if we suddenly decided that our people were so much influenced that public opinion polls were a menace.
There is now an international association of public opinion institutes which can and does poll 17 or more countries within 72 hours. The idea is that if a world-wide crisis develops an almost immediate reaction can be obtained. I think this international polling association was used during the Suez crisis. Dr. George Gallup of the United States was the founder of this international organization and in a speech he made last year he said this:
It takes courage, as well as ability, to stand up and be counted. The awful drubbing we pollsters received in this country-
He meant the United States.
-in 1948 is ample proof of this. Therefore,-
Dr. Gallup concluded.
-we salute those hardy souls who are willing to stake their reputation in this toughest of all fields of research, the prediction of human behaviour.
Incidentally, may I say that the hon. member for Timiskaming mentioned a figure of 3 per cent in speaking of the margin of error in the last United States election. I think it is much closer to .03 per cent. The margin of error was less than 1 per cent. This prediction of human behaviour is, I believe, big news especially around the time of an election. Hence the hon. member for Timiskaming is asking this government to legislate against the circulation of specific news.
I noticed that the hon. member kept throwing out innuendos about the integrity of polls and the objectivity of polls. I can only say that the polls, whether they be political or commercial, always have to prove themselves. If they are consistently wrong, no one will believe in them. As for objectivity, may I say that this is done all over the world. Anything of current interest-that is news, whether it is controversial or otherwise- must find its place in every worth-while poll. In our personal election campaigns we all conduct straw polls. Would this bill make it
[Miss Aitken. j
illegal for us to mention our findings from a platform and thence to the press?
The hon. member for Saint Antoine-West-mount (Mr. Webster) asked that question when we debated a similar bill in 1959. He asked: Are we to make this a crime? Are we to make it unlawful to mention from a platform predictions regarding our own election?
I know that most Toronto newspapers before an election send reporters right across the country with instructions to find out what people are thinking and how they are going to vote. These findings are always published in the newspapers before an election. Is this legitimate news gathering assignment also to become illegal? Indeed, Mr. Speaker, what people think and what people do are the two most important areas of news all over the world. Even to contemplate legislation against these facets of news is not only nonsense but dangerous nonsense.
As I said the last time we debated this subject, the mere introduction of this kind of bill by the socialists is a warning to the Canadian people. If this is what socialism would do if it should ever gain power, I say this: Let us be warned and see that socialism does not gain power.
This bill is definitely an infringement of freedom. It is a demonstration of gross arrogance in which the elected representatives would be saying to the Canadian people: You are so stupid that we must save you from yourselves and not let you know what your fellow Canadians are thinking.
The hon. member for Timiskaming, as reported at page 2898 of Hansard of April 21, 1959, said that publication of polls during an election:
-is eliminating one of the basic rights which the people possess-the right of choice.
If that is not an insult to the Canadian people, I do not know what is. He is saying that the elector is incapable of making up his own mind and that the thinking of others should not be published because then everyone would think the same way. I have a healthier respect than that for the elector's capacity to think for himself, and I shall certainly vote against this bill.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS
speechtext: I do not know anything about British Columbia; I have enough to do here. But I do say that I do not think I should ask the Minister of Justice, because I believe it is an infringement against the bill of rights in the freedom of the press clause.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that the hon. member who has just resumed her seat, by her own admission says she does not know much about British Columbia, and I am sure that British Columbians throughout the province would be quite pleased to have her visit the province at any time. We would benefit by that visit and I am sure the hon. member would also.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I just say that when I said I did not know much about British Columbia I was referring to her laws, not to her beauties.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS
speechtext:
I am quite sure from that statement that the hon. member realizes it is the most beautiful province in our nation.
I listened very carefully to what the hon. member who has just concluded her remarks said about this bill, and I think it is extremely unfortunate that the two members who have spoken had to resort to innuendo type accusations about the motives of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters') who introduced this bill.
There was the insinuation that it represented some desire to restrict the freedom of the press, to control people and to rigidly dominate them in some fascist type of way. This is, of course, just puerile silliness on the part of hon. members who use this type of argument which they know themselves is not valid. It is only designed to take up a bit of time so that we might not have to vote on this particular issue.
I can understand the views of the hon. member who just resumed her seat on this matter of public opinion polls and people who conduct public opinion polls, because of her very gentle affection and close relationship to an individual in Canada who participates in conducting this type of poll and who rigged a particular question at a poll in order to produce a particular answer and misinterpreted the results in order to prove a particular point. This was a misuse of a public opinion poll on the trading stamp issue, so I can understand what the hon. member says because of the gentle relationship which exists between her and this individual. I can understand that the hon. member would want to protect this sort of activity.
Canada Elections Act
I do not know whether or not they realize it, but I also understood both hon. members who spoke to condemn themselves quite roundly for doing precisely the same sort of thing that they now accuse my hon. friend for Timiskaming of trying to do. I will use their words. I think they are the wrong words to use, but these hon. members used them in this application and so I will use them also.
During the last session both of them supported wholeheartedly the idea of the restriction of people's rights, the idea of restricting the freedom of the press, the idea of rigidly controlling when particular radio broadcasts should be made when it came to election results. If one looked at the Elections Act, which we reviewed and revised and spent many hours on in the privileges and elections committee, and if he looks at the revisions we made-some changes were necessary because some things had not been changed for years-he would find, for instance, if I may use this as an example, that on election day it is completely contrary to the Elections Act to broadcast the results of an election in the eastern part of Canada when, because of the time zone difference, the election has not been completed in the western part of Canada.
It is illegal to report that sort of thing until the results are finally in from British Columbia and all across the nation. This is a restriction on the freedom of the press. The hon. members supported it without any qualms or hesitation at that time. They have supported year after year, practically every time the Elections Act has been amended, and again last year, the provision that restricted the press and radio in regard to using radio broadcasting for political purposes for a certain period of time before election day. That is a restriction on the press and certain individuals who want to get across their point of view. This attitude that has been taken is just silly nonsense, as I said a moment ago, levelling these accusations at the hon. member for Timiskaming.
They also supported this new legislation last year that we should not use certain kinds of radio stations to broadcast election material. This was endorsed unanimously by this house. It was a restriction on the right of an individual to use a particular radio broadcasting or television station in a federal election in order to get across points of view to the public.
This house endorsed that legislation, including the two members who have just sat down. The use of posters in our election headquarters. the use of buttons, ribbons, and so on

Canada Elections Act
to be worn on election day are all, in the words of the hon. members who have just completed their speeches, restrictions on the freedom and the rights of individuals, but they support those things unanimously.
They come into this matter now merely because one of the hon. members might disagree with my hon. friend for Timiskaming in another field, namely the field of divorce. They come along and drag out all these cliche phrases of "rigid, fascist type control", and it is just a lot of silly nonsense.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) first attacked the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) and then the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Pascoe) on what they said. He mentioned a list of restrictions that we have in the Elections Act. Practically all the restrictions he mentioned refer to the day voting takes place. This bill seeks to restrict certain publications from the day parliament is dissolved or the writs issued, and before. That is a considerable length of time.
Gallup polls of one form or another disseminate information. Before condemning or proposing a piece of legislation we should be familiar with its contents. I think previous speakers in this debate have laid particular stress on what effect this legislation would have on the press. But this bill goes further than that. It makes one guilty of an illegal practice under the Elections Act-and the penalties under that act are, I would say, pretty stiff-to do these things from the time parliament is dissolved, or the writs issued in the case of a by-election. As a matter of fact, it even refers to a vacancy in a constituency, I presume on account of the death of a member.
It prohibits Gallup polls or straw votes being broadcast over our radio-not only newspapers-by means of a news sheet or by means of a poster. I presume the law under this bill would go so far as to prohibit a class at school from putting up on a bulletin board the results of, call it a straw vote if you like, elections that schools are in the habit of taking amongst their students.
I think everyone is interested when an election is on. All parties are interested in the outcome. Notification must be given on billboards, in handbills or in some other manner. I presume anyone who took a straw vote could not even communicate it by way of a letter to his sweetheart. That is covering a lot of ground. That is a lot of prohibition. Nevertheless, this measure does not make it illegal to conduct such a poll, and if you could whisper the result around, if you could get the information around by

word of mouth, or from house to house and get away with it you would not be liable to be punished under the provisions of this bill.
I was very interested in what the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) had to say in his introductory remarks, and I tried to find the reason that prompted him to introduce this bill or what prompts him to introduce it annually. We have heard nothing on that score. We have not heard that any section of the Canadian people or any individuals have asked for the enactment of such a law as he proposes. The hon. member referred to the fact that the legislature of British Columbia has passed such a law prohibiting the publication of straw polls or Gallup polls. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) interjected that it was the Conservative party that did it. Well, it is a long time since British Columbia had a Conservative government.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS

I know the British Columbia legislature passed a bill prohibiting the publication of polls of this type in 1939 and I am going on the authority of the hon. member for Timiskaming who in his address to this house on April 21, 1959, said, as reported on page 2897 of Hansard:
British Columbia faced this matter in 1939 when they passed section 168 of the British Columbia elections act which reads:
"No person, corporation or organization shall after the issue of the writ for any election take any straw vote which will, prior to the election, distinguish the political opinions of the voters in any electoral district."
I have not had time to call for the British Columbia statutes but I know from memory, without calling on the statutes, that in 1939 there was a Social Credit government in British Columbia, and I have a recollection that a government of the same political colour in a sister province to the east had tried to censor the press by passing certain legislation-
I appreciate interruptions. I want to be set right if I am wrong in saying this was passed in 1939. I am only going on the authority of the hon. member for Timiskaming.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT PUBLICATION OF STRAW POLL RESULTS

and more controls. If we are going to control public opinion we might as well start by controlling the press. We might as well abolish the press gallery and keep the newspaper men out. We might as well censor everything they write. We might as well pass a law censoring everything that is said on radio and on television. We might as well censor everything. Then what? Mr. Speaker, then we would be nearer to that socialist heaven behind the iron curtain where everything is controlled.
